title: Chrysippus the builder
hookLine: the third head of the school built its logic; without Chrysippus, the ancients said, no Stoa (Diogenes Laërtius 7.183)

lines: NOBODY PUTS THE BUILDER ON A POSTER.
cards: Behind a lot of things that last, there's a quiet third person. Someone had the vision, someone had the heart, and then someone came along and built the thing: wrote the rules, fixed the plumbing, made it last.

That person rarely ends up on a poster. In the Stoic school, the visionary was Zeno, the heart was Cleanthes, and the builder was a long-distance runner from Asia Minor who wrote books by the hundreds.
The ancients had a saying about him.

teach.b: First, the saying. Diogenes Laërtius reports it in his Lives: if there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa. Without him, the school would have faded.

He came from Soli, in what's now southern Turkey, and is said to have trained as a runner before turning to philosophy. He studied under Cleanthes, and became the third head of the school. Second, what he built.
Zeno's ideas had come under heavy attack from rival schools, and Chrysippus gave them structure: definitions, arguments, answers to objections. Above all, logic.

teach.h: IF THIS, THEN THAT: STOIC LOGIC.
teach.b: He worked out a system for reasoning with whole statements: if this, then that; either this or that; not both. Modern logicians recognize it as an early form of what they call propositional logic. Third, his confidence.
A story says he told Cleanthes: just teach me the doctrines, and I'll find the proofs myself.
Diogenes says he wrote over seven hundred books. None survives whole. Like Zeno, he's known through quotations, many of them from opponents arguing against him.
Inspiration starts things. Structure keeps them alive.
Epictetus and Marcus stood on what Chrysippus built, and both mention him by name. A good habit works the same way. A feeling gets you started.
A small, steady structure, the same time, the same place, the same first step, gets you through the days you don't feel it.

how: Students of the Stoics know Chrysippus as the school's great systematizer, and historians of logic study his reconstructed system of reasoning with whole statements.

o: a Greek runner who won races at Olympia
the third Stoic head, who gave the school its logic
a rival philosopher who attacked Zeno's ideas

games.q: Chrysippus the builder. tap the pairs.

s: the ancients said that without Chrysippus there would be no Stoa
Diogenes Laërtius reports the saying in his Lives, book seven.
several of Chrysippus's seven hundred books survive
none survives whole; we know him through quotations and scraps, often from opponents.
modern logicians see in his work an early form of propositional logic
he reasoned with whole statements: if, or, and not.

games.q: you're a young student of Cleanthes, sure of yourself. what does the story say Chrysippus told his teacher?
o: teach me the doctrines and the proofs, slowly.
just teach me the doctrines; I'll find the proofs myself.
I'm leaving to found my own school.
games.why: he asked only for the doctrines and promised to supply the arguments himself. building the arguments became his life's work.

practice: Think of one thing you care about that keeps slipping: a walk, a call to your mother, this practice, reading. Give it one small structure, plain and logical, the way Chrysippus would: if this, then that.
If I pour my coffee, then I sit for two minutes; if I park the car, then I call. Pick the trigger and the step, and say the sentence to yourself once, clearly.

wordCard.voice: Chrysippus. The third head of the Stoic school, who gave it logic and structure; without him, the ancients said, there'd be no Stoa. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: logic, the study of reasoning. For the Stoics, one of philosophy's three parts, with physics and ethics.

carryVoice: Your line: the builder. No Chrysippus, the ancients said, no Stoa. Day six hundred forty-three, done.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
